name: Bees
description: Here's some information about bees which are very important to the environment and some things we can do to help them thrive.
longDescription: Bees are insects known as pollinators. Western honeybees are well known for producing honey, and pollination of flowers, fruits, and vegetables. Most crops require insect pollination in order to produce seeds. Bees live in colonies, also known as hives. This is where they reproduce and make honey to store for the winter. Honeybees fly extremely fast, and beat their wings around 200 times per second. Unfortunately, bees are declining at an alarming rate due to viruses, climate change, decreasing crop diversity, and loss of habitat. Reducing the use of pesticides and diminishing the effects of climate change will help these important pollinators to repopulate. You can help increase the bee population by planting native shrubs and flowers that in your yard. Recently, beekeeping has become an interesting and popular hobby.

name: Butterflies
description: Here's some information about butterflies.
longDescription: Butterflies and moths are pollinators of plant and food sources for other animals. They make up the second largest order of insects. Butterflies have thousands of tiny overlapping scales covering their wings. Each scale is a single color and collectively these scales create the complex color patterns seen on their wings. Monarch butterflies are facing extinction. Populations in the last ten years have declined by over 90%. Butterflies in general are in trouble, but with just a few nectar and hosts plants you can attract and sustain dozens of butterfly species. Limiting the use of insecticides and herbicides will also help to increase their population.

name: Rain Garden
description: The rain garden collects water which runs off from different parts of the park. Our rain garden hosts many native plants and small wildlife.
longDescription: This rain garden collects stormwater from the park. Also known as a bioretention basin, runoff that originates from rain, snow, hail, and sleet are diverted via underground pipes into this rain garden and soak into the soil. Rain gardens, such as this, are effective in removing up to 90% of nutrients and chemicals and up to 80% of sediments before they enter a water body. This garden will look dry most of the time, but will accumulate water during storm events and will drain within 12 to 48 hours, thereby cleaning the water before it enters the Little Neshaminy Watershed. Native plants and wildflowers are typically planted in rain gardens.

name: Monarch Way Station
longDescription: Monarch Waystations are places that provide resources necessary for monarchs to produce successive generations and sustain their migration. Without milkweeds throughout their spring and summer breeding areas in North America, monarchs would not be able to produce the successive generations that culminate in the migration each fall. Similarly, without nectar from flowers these fall migratory monarch butterflies would be unable to make their long journey to overwintering grounds in Mexico. The need for host plants for larvae and energy sources for adults applies to all monarch and butterfly populations around the world.
